These orders totaled a staggering 295,950,000 shares for which Scout Trading was not long 
the requisite number of shares at the time of submission.1 The magnitude of the deficit was 
extraordinary, with the firm short more than 1.1 million shares per redemption order on 
average.1 Within just the first two months of the applicable period under NASDAQ jurisdiction, 
Scout submitted at least 38 naked redemption orders totaling 15.7 million shares.1 
The sheer volume of Scout Trading’s naked shorting single-handedly compromised the 
integrity of the underlying ETFs, triggering regulatory tripwires designed to identify systemic 
market manipulation.1 Under Regulation SHO, a security that experiences excessive fails to 
deliver for five consecutive settlement days is placed on the "Threshold Securities List," 
subjecting it to severe trading restrictions across all broker-dealers.1 The regulatory findings 
explicitly noted that Bleich’s trading strategy was a "significant factor" in forcing the 14 ETFs 
under review to be classified as Threshold Securities for sustained timeframes.1 
To illustrate the unprecedented market dominance of this abusive strategy, FINRA isolated 
Scout Trading's activity in the FAZ ETF (Direxion Daily Financial Bear 3X Shares).1 During the 
investigative period, Bleich’s firm accounted for approximately 95 percent of its clearing firm's 
total fails in FAZ.1 More alarmingly, Scout Trading alone was responsible for approximately 59 
percent of the aggregate total market fails to deliver in FAZ across all market participants in the 
entire United States.1 This staggering concentration of settlement failures by a single firm 
caused FAZ to remain on the Threshold List for more than 250 consecutive settlement dates 
from March 7, 2011, through March 16, 2012.1 By distorting the supply and demand dynamics of 
the ETF ecosystem to this degree, Bleich's firm engaged in behavior that fundamentally 
threatened the orderly function of the secondary markets.1 
4. Secondary Compliance Deficiencies and the 
Erasure of Supervisory Infrastructure 
Compounding the severity of the trading violations was FINRA's determination that Scout 
Trading operated in a state of near-total supervisory negligence.1 The investigation found that 
the firm violated NASDAQ Rules 3010 and 2110 because it completely failed to establish, 
maintain, and enforce a supervisory system.1 Scout Trading lacked any written supervisory 
procedures (WSPs) specifically designed to ensure compliance with Rule 204 of Regulation 
SHO.1 This absolute absence of oversight cannot be dismissed as a mere administrative error; 
rather, it indicates a structural prioritization of revenue generation over regulatory adherence.1 
While the $3 million FINRA/NASDAQ Regulation SHO fine represents the apex of Bleich’s 
regulatory exposure, an exhaustive analysis of Scout Trading’s historical records via FINRA 
BrokerCheck reveals a broader, systemic pattern of chronic compliance deficiencies enforced 
by the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE).1
